entry.title: Author Meghan O’Rourke on What It Means to Live Well with Chronic Illness

media:group.media:title: Author Meghan O’Rourke on What It Means to Live Well with Chronic Illness
media:group.media:description:
Dean Lloyd Minor welcomes Meghan O’Rourke, poet, journalist and author of “The Invisible Kingdom: Reimagining Chronic Illness,” for a conversation about living with chronic illness and the search for answers when symptoms defy easy diagnosis. Drawing on O’Rourke’s personal experience, they discuss the importance of acknowledging uncertainty, listening to patients, and recognizing their suffering, as well as how the COVID-19 pandemic has brought greater visibility to immune-mediated illnesses. They also explore the challenges of delivering coordinated care and lessons chronic illness offers for precision medicine, quality of life and living well when a condition cannot simply be cured.
To learn more about The Minor Consult podcast, visit https://med.stanford.edu/minorconsult
About The Minor Consult Podcast The Minor Consult explores what it means to be a great leader today. Hosted by Stanford School of Medicine Dean Lloyd Minor, MD, the podcast convenes top minds from across fields to share their perspectives, impart lessons from their careers, and discuss the complex challenges that leaders face. Through their conversations, Dr. Minor unearths the qualities and skills that help leaders to succeed.
Dr. Minor has served as Dean since 2012 and is also a professor of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery at the Stanford School of Medicine. Under his leadership, Stanford Medicine has emerged as a leader in the Precision Health revolution, which emphasizes preventive, personalized health care and leverages advances in biomedicine to treat and cure complex diseases. With more than 160 published articles and chapters, Dr. Minor is an expert in balance and inner ear disorders. In 2012, he was elected to the National Academy of Medicine.

entry.title: Walk With Me: Karen Adams, gynecologist advancing menopause care and healthy aging

media:group.media:title: Walk With Me: Karen Adams, gynecologist advancing menopause care and healthy aging
media:group.media:description:
Meet Karen Adams, MD, a gynecologist at Stanford Medicine and director of the Stanford Program in Menopause & Healthy Aging whose work focuses on improving care for women through menopause and beyond. Hear what drew her to women’s health, what she’s learned from more than 30 years of caring for patients — and a few things about who she is outside the clinic.
Adams is a clinical professor of obstetrics and gynecology and the Farwell Family Director of the Stanford Program in Menopause & Healthy Aging. She is board-certified in obstetrics and gynecology and lifestyle medicine and is a Menopause Society-certified menopause practitioner.

media:group.media:description:
Stanford Medicine microbiologist Justin Sonnenburg explains how the trillions of microbes in our gut shape our health, why fiber matters so much, and which gut health trends hold up.
Learn more: The gut-brain connection: What the science says: https://stan.md/4Arv1BG Gut microbes across continents trace ancient human migration: https://stan.md/4zzh04N Untangling the complex connections between the gut, brain and microbiome: https://stan.md/3WDIXd9 Gut bust: https://stan.md/4zHSv5B
Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, professor of microbiology and immunology, is leading experts on the human gut microbiome and how it influences health. His research explores how diet — particularly dietary fiber — shapes the trillions of microbes that live in our digestive system and, in turn, impact metabolism, immune function, inflammation and overall well-being. media:group.media:description:
How does the body change during perimenopause and menopause? Stanford Medicine gynecologist Karen Adams, MD, explains what happens during this transition, explores treatment options and shares how women can navigate midlife and prioritize their long-term health.
Learn more about menopause and Karen Adam's work: Taking on the menopause, breast cancer double whammy: https://stan.md/4BHTsw2 Mental health and menopause: There are connections and solutions: https://stan.md/4zunTEu Ask me anything: Menopause: https://stan.md/4sH3rxt
Karen Adams, MD, clinical professor of obstetrics and gynecology, is director of the Menopause & Healthy Aging program and a nationally recognized expert in menopause, women’s midlife health, and lifestyle medicine. Her work focuses on helping women navigate the physical, emotional, and cognitive changes of perimenopause and menopause using the latest evidence-based treatments and preventive strategies. Adams explains what happens during the menopausal transition, separates myths from facts about hormone therapy and other treatments, and discusses common concerns including hot flashes, sleep disruption, mood changes, weight gain, sexual health, and long-term risks to bone and cardiovascular health.

media:group.media:title: Oura CEO Tom Hale on How Wearables and AI Are Moving Care Beyond the Clinic
media:group.media:description:
Dean Lloyd Minor welcomes Tom Hale, CEO of Oura, for a conversation about how wearable technology can help people take a more active role in their health. They discuss how an individual’s biometric data can inform everyday habits, how wearables could help clinicians identify health risks earlier, and the potential for AI to make care more proactive and personalized. Together, they explore a potential future in which continuous health monitoring could help flag risks before symptoms appear, providing more opportunities to predict and prevent disease.

entry.title: Optogenetics Explained: The Science Behind the 2026 Nobel Prize | Stanford Medicine

media:group.media:title: Optogenetics Explained: The Science Behind the 2026 Nobel Prize | Stanford Medicine
media:group.media:description:
Karl Deisseroth, MD, PhD, is a pioneer of optogenetics, a groundbreaking technique that uses light to control specific cells in the brain and has transformed scientists’ ability to study how the brain drives sensation, thought, decision-making and behavior.
Over nearly two decades, Deisseroth and his team have helped develop and advance the field, identifying new light-sensitive proteins called opsins and uncovering how their structures allow researchers to precisely influence neural activity with light.
Deisseroth, a Stanford professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences, was one of three scientists awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in optogenetics. Bioengineering is a department jointly run by the Schools of Medicine and Engineering.
Learn more: https://stan.md/4yavQNG https://stan.md/4jdXmGj
